raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old, otherwise healthy, male was admitted to the emergency room with a four-day history of malaise, myalgia, and high-grade fever. Laboratory tests showed increased liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 2216 U/L and alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 1611 U/L), but normal bilirubin. Dengue Fever (DF) rapid test (NS1) and serology (ELISA IgM and IgG) were performed with negative results. Two days later the patient developed jaundice (total bilirubin 6.36 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 5.60 mg/dL) with a decrease in platelet count (52000 /mm3), normal international normalized ratio (INR) (0.85), and moderate proteinuria. At that time, abdominal ultrasonography showed hepatomegaly. Serology for viral hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus, and Cytomegalovirus were negative. Dengue serology was repeated, and found positive, suggesting DF-related hepatitis. Despite an uncertain patient report of prior YF vaccination, YF polymerase chain reaction (YF-PCR) was performed considering the epidemiological risk and YF outbreak context. The patient was discharged after one week with improvement of laboratorial parameters (AST 259 U/L, ALT 638 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 153 U/L, platelets 294000 /mm3, and total bilirubin 2.25 mg/dL). The YF-PCR result was not available prior to discharge.
After 40 days, he was readmitted to the hospital with persistent fatigue, jaundice, and pruritus. Liver enzymes and bilirubin had increased (total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL, AST 1037 U/L, ALT 2289 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase [GGT] 669 U/L, and INR 1.05). Extensive workup including serologies, ceruloplasmin, and ferritin was performed, but not indicative of a specific etiology. A hypothesis of autoimmune liver disorder was discarded by negative autoantibodies (i.e., anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle, and anti-mitochondria antibodies) and normal serum gamma-globulin. Liver biopsy demonstrated lobular hepatitis with mild neutrophilic infiltration (Figure 1). The remaining parenchymal cells showed frequent hepatocyte ballooning, macro- and microvacuolar steatosis, and rare apoptotic bodies. The patient was discharged again after a small decrease in total bilirubin without a definitive diagnosis. A follow-up hepatology appointment was scheduled for five days later. 
Upon hepatologist consultation, it was found that the YF-PCR ordered during the first hepatitis episode was positive, thus corroborating the suspicion of relapsing hepatitis due to YF. A pathological review was performed, including YF virus immunohistochemistry stain, but it was negative. The patient was started on ursodeoxycholic acid (10 mg/kg) and within three days improved his pruritus and bilirubin levels. In the two-week follow-up period, liver enzymes were normal, and the medication was suspended.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with malaise, myalgia, and high-grade fever for 4 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency room with a 4-day history of high-grade fever, generalized myalgia, and malaise. Two days after admission, he developed jaundice, moderate proteinuria, and worsening thrombocytopenia. His transaminases gradually improved, and he was discharged after 1 week. Forty days later, he was readmitted due to persistent fatigue, worsening scleral icterus, and intense pruritus, with severe rebound in transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Uncertain documentation of prior arboviral immunization. Epidemiological exposure: lived/worked in an area experiencing an active viral epidemic.
subjective.review_of_systems: High-grade fever, malaise, diffuse myalgia, fatigue, jaundice, and intense generalized pruritus.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: clinical jaundice; abdominal palpation revealed hepatomegaly. Readmission at day 40: deep jaundice, excoriations secondary to pruritus, persistent fatigue; no stigmata of chronic liver disease.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: AST 2216 U/L, ALT 1611 U/L, normal total bilirubin. Day 2: total bilirubin 6.36 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.60 mg/dL, platelet count 52,000/mm3, international normalized ratio (INR) 0.85, moderate proteinuria. Discharge (day 7): AST 259 U/L, ALT 638 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 153 U/L, platelets 294,000/mm3, total bilirubin 2.25 mg/dL. Readmission (day 40): total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL, AST 1037 U/L, ALT 2289 U/L, GGT 669 U/L, INR 1.05. Abdominal ultrasound: hepatomegaly. Serologies: Dengue rapid test (NS1) and ELISA IgM/IgG negative on day 1; repeat dengue serology later positive (cross-reactive flavivirus antibody). Viral hepatitis panel (hepatitis A, B, C), Epstein-Barr virus, and Cytomegalovirus serologies: negative. Autoimmune markers (anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial antibodies): negative; normal serum gamma-globulin; ceruloplasmin and ferritin not indicative of a specific etiology.
objective.advanced_workup: Percutaneous liver biopsy (second admission): lobular hepatitis with mild neutrophilic infiltration, diffuse hepatocyte ballooning, macro- and microvacuolar steatosis, and rare apoptotic bodies. Immunohistochemical staining for specific viral antigen on liver tissue was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of relapsing hepatitis due to Yellow Fever: Serum RT-PCR obtained during the initial acute hepatitis episode was positive for Yellow Fever virus RNA. Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C, EBV, CMV) and autoimmune liver diseases were ruled out by negative serologies and autoantibodies. Pathological review confirmed lobular hepatitis with steatosis and apoptotic bodies, though immunohistochemistry was negative on late biopsy. Treatment: The patient was initiated on oral ursodeoxycholic acid 10 mg/kg daily; pruritus and bilirubin improved within 3 days. Transaminases completely normalized at 2-week follow-up, and ursodeoxycholic acid was successfully discontinued.
